args.topic: Tenant's liability for damage to the premises
Landlord's notice of claim on the deposit

content:
Whether you owe the $85 turns on one lease clause, and on your facts that point is not settled.

The $85. Each resident is "jointly and severally liable" for damage to the unit's shared appliances "when Landlord cannot determine which resident caused the damage," and the charge "will be divided equally" (Lease Section 3.4). The same clause says you are not responsible for a roommate's rent. The lease is the only source I have for how roommates share a charge like this.

A washer the four of you use fits "shared appliances," and the lease lists the washer among the appliances the landlord furnishes (Lease Section 7.1). You confirmed the office says it cannot tell who caused it, so it split the charge. Devin's admission in the group chat is something you said here, not a confirmed fact, and nothing you confirmed says the landlord knows it.

So the answer turns on what Section 3.4 leaves open:
- If the landlord cannot determine who caused it, the clause puts an equal share on you even though Devin broke it.
- If the landlord can determine it, the clause's words no longer reach the charge, and the clause does not say who pays then.
Section 3.4 does not say what it takes for the landlord to "determine" who caused the damage, so I cannot say which side you are on. Devin's admission is the fact this point turns on.

Late fees. The only late charge clause the search found is written about rent: "If any installment is not received by 11:59 p.m. on the fifth (5th) day of the month," a late charge starts at $50.00 (Lease Section 3.2). Installments are the rent payments (Lease Section 3.1), and you confirmed you paid rent. The tool found no lease wording that applies that late charge to a charge that is not a rent installment, and the statute text I have has nothing on late fees. So a late fee on the $85 would not rest on what Section 3.2 says on its words.

The deposit. The lease lets the landlord deduct "late charges," "Resident's equal share of damage to the shared areas of the Unit under Section 3.4," and "any other amount due under this Lease" (Lease Section 4.2). If you owe the $85 under Section 3.4, that clause lets the office take it from the deposit; if you do not owe it, the clause does not reach it.

The statute sets how a claim is made. The landlord must give written notice of its claim, by certified mail or e-mail, within 30 days after the rental agreement ends, and you then have 15 days after you receive it to object in writing (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). A landlord that misses the 30 days "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit," but may still sue for damages after returning it (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). If you do not object in time, the landlord may deduct the claim, and that "does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(b)). This changes only if you move out before the term ends. Whether it applies turns on your lease's own term on notice before moving out (Lease Section 9.2). If it applies and you do not give that notice, the landlord is relieved of the claim notice (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)).

Cases.
Multach v. Adams, 418 So. 2d 1254, 1255 (Fla. 4th DCA 1982), read the 1981 statute. A commercial tenant who put holes in the building was liable because the damage was "contrary to the express terms of the lease." Its facts differ from yours: one tenant, a commercial lease, damage he did himself. It cuts against you only in that a court enforced a lease's terms on damage, and your lease has Section 3.4. It says nothing about roommates.
Durene v. Alcime, 448 So. 2d 1208, 1210 (Fla. 3d DCA 1984), read the 1981 text. A landlord that missed the deposit claim notice "forfeited his access" to the deposit, which "may not be used for purposes of a set-off," though it could still bring a separate claim for damages. Its tenant had moved out and sued for the deposit; you have not. It helps you only if the landlord's notice is late, and it does not stop a suit over the $85. Plakhov v. Serova distinguished it where the tenant had not given the early move-out notice.
Malagon v. Solari, 566 So. 2d 352, 354 (Fla. 4th DCA 1990), read the 1989 text and follows Durene. Damages the landlord won on a counterclaim could not be a setoff against the deposit where the landlord had not given the required notice, and it noted the landlord's liability for fees under 83.49(3)(c). Its tenants had already sued. Fees under 83.49(3)(c) go to the prevailing party, so they can run against you too.
Casey v. Picinich, 573 So. 2d 76, 77 (Fla. 4th DCA 1990), read the 1987 text: an "untimely notice forfeited their right to impose any claim" on the deposit. It is a small-sum case on a late notice, it matches Durene, and it says nothing on who caused damage.
Plakhov v. Serova, 126 So. 3d 1221, 1223 (Fla. 4th DCA 2012): the landlord's duty to send the claim notice "was excused by the Tenant's failure" to give the seven-day notice before leaving early, so the landlord could apply the deposit against what the tenant owed. That cuts against a tenant who leaves early without the notice. You have not said you are leaving early, so it matters only if that changes.

Showing the office Devin's messages may not stop the split. I have to add a clause I had not found in my last answer, and it cuts against you.

Two lease clauses bear on this, and the lease does not say which controls where they overlap:
- Section 3.4 is the clause for shared appliances. Its equal split applies "when Landlord cannot determine which resident caused the damage," and it says you are "not responsible for the rent of any roommate" (Lease Section 3.4). Each roommate signs a separate lease (Lease Section 1.3). On this reading, if Devin's messages let the office determine who caused it, the four-way split loses its basis.
- Section 7.4 says you "shall pay for the repair of damage caused by Resident, a roommate, or their guests, including clogged drains and damage to appliances from misuse" (Lease Section 7.4). The write-up you confirmed says "resident misuse." On this reading, proof that Devin caused it does not take you out of paying; it only shows who caused it.

I cannot say which reading holds, so I cannot tell you the office cannot split it four ways. Your screenshots bear on the condition in Section 3.4. They do not answer Section 7.4.

What you can do. The two options the tool checks for the washer, ending the lease and not paying rent over it, are both closed on your facts, because you confirmed the problem was caused on your side (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1); Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b); Fla. Stat. 83.51(4)). Neither is about the $85, and the tool has no option for disputing a charge. So what follows is what the lease and the stored statute say about each choice.
- Not pay it for now. The office named late fees and the deposit. The late charge clause the search found is written about rent installments (Lease Section 3.2). The deposit route needs the landlord's written claim notice within 30 days after the rental agreement ends, and you then have 15 days to object in writing (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). A landlord that misses that notice loses the deposit as a source but may still sue (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). The tool has not read whether your lease treats an unpaid charge like unpaid rent: the tool found nothing for "as rent" in the lease's text, and Section 3.4 names "the Rent and charges" separately.
- Send the office Devin's messages in writing. A notice from you must be in writing and delivered by hand to the leasing office, sent by certified mail, or sent by e-mail (Lease Section 13.1). This goes to the Section 3.4 condition and does not settle the Section 7.4 reading. The tool found no procedure in the lease's text for disputing a charge; "dispute" and "object" found nothing.
- Pay it. Then there is nothing left for the office to deduct from the deposit for this charge (Lease Section 4.2). The lease clauses I found do not say how roommates settle up with each other afterward.

args.topic: Conditions caused by the tenant under 83.51(4)

content:
Not necessarily. Devin breaking the washer does not by itself end the landlord's duty to fix what is still wrong, but your lease has an exception that may reach part of it.

The rule. The landlord must keep the washer "in good working order and repair," "except for damage caused by Resident, a roommate, or their guests" (Lease Section 7.1). For the statute's duties, the landlord is not responsible for "conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.51(4)).

Applied. It turns on what is causing the leak now. If the leak is part of the damage Devin caused, the exception applies. If it is there because the repair was not done right, it is not damage a roommate caused, and Section 7.1 still binds the landlord. The write-up you confirmed says "resident misuse," and you say the repair was not done right. The lease does not say which counts, and the tool does not know the cause; a technician or an inspection could say. What you just told me is not confirmed yet. The sheet asks you next, and until then the tool's record still says the problem was caused on your side.

Can you make them fix it. The tool has no option that orders a repair. Its two options on the washer are both closed as the record stands, because of that confirmed cause (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1) to end the lease; Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b) to not pay rent). If the sheet records that the leak was not caused on your side, they would be:
- Ending the lease. The landlord's duty here comes from the lease's repair clause, which 83.56(1) reaches as "material provisions of the rental agreement." It would still need a written notice that names the problem and says you intend to end the lease, then 7 days after delivery without a fix (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). You confirmed your requests did not say that. Two points stay open. Whether paying rent waived this is not settled: if an unfixed leak is a continuing noncompliance, paying rent does not waive it; if the noncompliance is the failure to fix a problem you already knew of, it does (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). And the statute does not define "material," so whether a small leak is one is not settled: it may turn on the kind of duty, or on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living in the unit.
- Not paying rent. This reaches only a failure of a duty in 83.51(1), not a lease promise alone (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). You confirmed the washer is not structure or plumbing, so it would turn on a building, housing, or health code that covers it. The tool holds no codes; the city or county code enforcement office can say. It also needs a written notice that says you intend not to pay rent, then 7 days (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)).
- Damages. "The aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.55). That is money, not an order to repair, and the tool does not work out an amount.

Notice. Your repair requests went in through the portal. The lease says a maintenance request "is a request for service and is not by itself a notice under Section 13.1" (Lease Section 7.2). A written notice goes by hand to the leasing office, by certified mail, or by e-mail (Lease Section 13.1). The 7 days in both options start only from such a notice that states the intention, and the program's deadlines show none running now. The lease also lists "an active water leak" as an emergency to report on the after-hours line (Lease Section 7.2); it does not say whether a small leak is one.

Cases, each beside your facts.
Charlemagne v. Francis, 700 So. 2d 157, 160 (Fla. 4th DCA 1997), read the 1993 text: 83.51(4) "is applicable only to exclude liability of the landlord under section 83.51," and there was "no evidence presented as to the cause" of the carpet ridges. A tenant fell on a carpet; you have a leaking washer. It matches on a disputed cause. The court called that exclusion "absolute," which cuts against you if Devin's damage is the cause, but it also shows a court wanting evidence of who caused the condition.
Mansur v. Eubanks, 401 So. 2d 1328, 1330 (Fla. 1981), read the 1977 text: the landlord has "a continuing duty to exercise reasonable care to repair dangerous defective conditions upon notice of their existence by the tenant, unless waived by the tenant." Its facts were a gas explosion, so it speaks to dangerous defects; whether a small leak is one is not known. K.D. Lewis Enterprises Corp. v. Smith distinguishes it as not creating a new tort claim for lost value of the premises.
Bennett M. Lifter, Inc. v. Varnado, 480 So. 2d 1336, 1341 (Fla. 3d DCA 1985), read the 1983 text: Mansur "did not purport to exonerate the landlord from responsibility for faulty injury-producing conditions which are not inherently dangerous." Its water heater was out three days after a report, like your unfixed request, but a child was burned; you describe no injury. Smith v. Grove Apartments follows it.
Smith v. Grove Apartments, LLC, 976 So. 2d 582, 586 (Fla. 3d DCA 2007), read the 2007 text: a "continuing statutory duty to maintain common areas in a safe condition and to repair dangerous, defective conditions upon notice of their existence, unless otherwise agreed to by the tenant." It matches you on repeated complaints that got no action. It differs: a parking lot and an injured tenant, and yours is an appliance in your unit. The dissent disagreed on the duty's reach.
Paterson v. Deeb, 472 So. 2d 1210, 1216 (Fla. 1st DCA 1985), read the 1981 text: "A landlord's violation of the act is at least evidence of negligence." A tenant was attacked after her lock and lighting requests were refused; yours is a leak with no injury. It enforces duties the statute states, and the statute text I have does not list a washer, so your washer claim rests on Section 7.1, not on this case. Menendez distinguishes it as based on an express statutory provision.
Bennett v. Mattison, 382 So. 2d 873, 875 (Fla. 1st DCA 1980), read the 1977 text: a violation of the common-area duty "would be evidence of negligence." A fall in a hallway; not a washer in your unit.
Haynes v. Lloyd, 533 So. 2d 944, 945 (Fla. 5th DCA 1988): the common-area duty "is not particularly relevant here" because it restates the common law duty. Broken glass hurt a child; a dissent disagreed. It does not reach your facts and, if anything, narrows reliance on that duty.
Solomon v. Gentry, 388 So. 2d 52, 53 (Fla. 4th DCA 1980), read the 1979 text: "no such warranty arises under a lease of real property" for fitness for a specific purpose. A heater was repaired and a fire followed. It cuts against a claim that a repair carried an implied promise to work; yours rests on the lease's repair clause.
Ray v. Tampa Windridge Associates, 596 So. 2d 676, 677 (Fla. 2d DCA 1991), read the 1985 text: the court assumed an agreement could relieve the landlord of a duty, then read the signed release and found it did not. Locks and an assault, not a washer. It shows a court reading the lease clause's own words, so the words of Section 7.1's exception decide whether it reaches your leak.
Menendez v. Palms West Condo. Ass'n, 736 So. 2d 58, 62 (Fla. 1st DCA 1999): no lease liability where "the lease contained no provision that either expressly or by implication required" the doorscope. A shooting. Your lease names the washer in Section 7.1, which differs in your favor, subject to its exception.

args.topic: Tenant's notice of the landlord's noncompliance

content:
The tool has no option that orders a repair. With your update, its two options on the washer now turn on points you can act on, and your portal requests are repair requests, not the notice either option needs.

Ending the lease (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)) is not settled. The landlord's duty comes from the lease's repair clause (Lease Section 7.1), which 83.56(1) reaches as "material provisions of the rental agreement," and the leak is no longer marked as caused on your side. What stays open is whether paying rent waived this (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). The statute does not settle it. One reading: a leak the landlord still has not fixed is a continuing noncompliance, so paying rent does not waive ending the lease, and the option is open. The other: the noncompliance is the failure to fix a problem you already knew of, so paying rent with that knowledge waives it, and the option is closed. The statute also does not define "material," so whether a small leak is one is not settled either.

Not paying rent (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)) is not known yet. It reaches only a failure of a duty in 83.51(1), not a lease promise alone. You confirmed the washer is not structure or plumbing, so it turns on a building, housing, or health code that covers it. You can check that: the city or county code enforcement office can say whether one does, and can inspect the unit. If one does, the option is open; if not, it is closed.

Damages are a third route outside the tool's options: "the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.55). That is money, not an order to repair, and the tool does not work out an amount.

Do the portal requests count. As repair requests, yes: the lease says to report a repair need through the portal (Lease Section 7.2). As a notice, no: a maintenance request "is a request for service and is not by itself a notice under Section 13.1" (Lease Section 7.2). The program's step list shows a written notice as done, but both options need a notice that also states an intention, to end the lease or not to pay rent (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1); Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)), and you confirmed neither request said that. So the next step in either option is a new written notice. The program's deadlines show no 7 days running, because they start only from delivery of that notice.

What the notice has to say. For ending the lease: it names the problem and says you intend to end the lease because of it (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). For not paying rent: it names the problem and says you intend not to pay rent because of it (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). A letter that only asks for the repair is a request, not either notice.

How to send it. Your lease says a notice from you must be in writing and delivered by hand to the leasing office, sent by certified mail to that address, or sent by e-mail to the office address (Lease Section 13.1). The statute is narrower on e-mail: a notice may go by e-mail only "if the parties have signed an addendum" agreeing to electronic delivery (Fla. Stat. 83.505(1)), and the tool has not seen one. You can check whether you signed one. Whether the lease's e-mail line can stand without that addendum is not settled by the stored text; 83.47(1)(a) makes a lease term void "to the extent that it purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part," and whether that reaches this is not something I can say. Hand delivery and certified mail are the two routes that do not depend on it.

What I need from you to draft it, because the letter is built by the program from your choices and I cannot write its text: which notice you want (a repair request only, one that also says you intend to end the lease, or one that also says you intend not to pay rent), how many days you give them to reply, and how you will deliver it.

Cases.
K.D. Lewis Enterprises Corp. v. Smith, 445 So. 2d 1032, 1037 (Fla. 5th DCA 1984), read the 1981 text: "To recover for diminishment in the value of the premises, it is necessary for the tenant to comply with section 83.56." Its tenants withheld rent over upkeep and lost possession when they did not pay into the court's registry; one tenant's clothes were damaged by a closet leak. It matches you on unrepaired upkeep and shows the 83.56 notice is what a claim for lost value needs. It also says that where a tenant's property is injured by the landlord's negligence, the claim "requires no notice under the statute," which could reach damage the leak does to your belongings. It cuts against withholding rent without the notice. Another case follows it, First Hanover v. Vazquez, and it limits Freedman v. Geiger to its facts.
Lakeway Management Co. of Florida v. Stolowilsky, 527 So. 2d 950, 951 (Fla. 3d DCA 1988), read the 1985 text: tenants who stopped paying rent made their first written complaint only after the landlord's three-day notice, so it was too late "to urging constructive eviction," and the court held the defense should not have been allowed. They had left and stopped paying rent; you have paid. It shows a court treating the timing of the tenant's written complaint as a condition for a defense, which is why a written notice before any dispute over rent matters.

The letter can name the $85, but weigh one thing first, because the same screenshots cut two ways.

What you have settled: the issue is the repair, you want them to fix the leak, you give them 7 days to reply, and you will deliver it by hand. Your lease allows that route: a notice from you may be "delivered by hand to the leasing office at 2600 SW Hartwell Lane, Gainesville, Florida 32608" (Lease Section 13.1). "Repair request only" is the posture called preserve: "Describes the condition and asks for the repair. Cites nothing." It states no intention to end the lease or stop paying rent, so it starts no 7-day period under either option (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1); Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). The 7 days are the time you give them to reply.

The $85. The letter tool writes a letter for one issue, and your matter holds only the repair. The $85 charge is not an issue the tool holds, so the letter has no part written for it. The line for what you want the landlord to do takes plain words, so the charge could go there. The program sends nothing and attaches nothing, so the screenshots would be yours to attach.

Weigh this. The screenshots show a roommate caused the damage. That is the fact Section 7.1's exception turns on, since the landlord need not repair "damage caused by Resident, a roommate, or their guests" (Lease Section 7.1). It is also the fact Section 7.4 turns on, where you "shall pay for the repair of damage caused by Resident, a roommate, or their guests" (Lease Section 7.4). And it is the fact the equal split turns on, "when Landlord cannot determine which resident caused the damage" (Lease Section 3.4). So the same screenshots may help you on the $85 and give the office a reason to say the washer is not its to repair. You told the tool the leak is the landlord's unfinished repair, a separate point from what Devin did, and one letter would put both in front of the office. Which way that goes, the lease does not say.

Do you want the letter to ask for the repair only, or for the repair and the $85 charge too?
